summary: When the disciples turn away people bringing children, Jesus is displeased, welcomes the children, takes them in His arms and blesses them.
key_insight: Mark says Jesus was “greatly displeased.” It is the only time the Gospels use this word for Jesus’ own feelings. What stirred Him was not His enemies but His own disciples standing between Him and the children.
story: People were bringing little children to Jesus, even infants, {Lk} so that He might put His hands on them and pray. {Mt} But the disciples rebuked those who brought them. {Mk}
When Jesus saw it, He was greatly displeased. {Mk} He called the children to Him {Lk} and said, “Let the little children come to Me, and do not forbid them; for of such is the kingdom of God.”
“Assuredly, I say to you, whoever does not receive the kingdom of God as a little child will by no means enter it.” {Mk}
Then He took them up in His arms, laid His hands on them, and blessed them. {Mk} Afterward He departed from there. {Mt}
differences: Luke calls them “infants”; Matthew and Mark say “little children.”
Matthew says the people wanted Jesus to put His hands on the children and pray; Mark and Luke say “that He might touch them.”
Only Mark says Jesus was “greatly displeased” and took the children up in His arms.
Mark and Luke include the saying about receiving the kingdom “as a little child”; Matthew records a similar saying earlier (Matthew 18:3).

scene.label: Hands and blessing
scene.text: Laying hands on a child with prayer was an old way of blessing, going back to Jacob blessing Joseph’s sons (Genesis 48:14–16). Later Jewish writings speak of parents bringing children to elders and teachers for such a blessing.

scene.label: Infants
scene.text: Luke’s word means babies, the same word he uses for John leaping in Elizabeth’s womb and for the Babe in the manger (Luke 1:41; 2:12, 16). Some of these children had to be carried to Jesus.

scene.label: Why the disciples objected
scene.text: The Gospels do not say. Jesus was on His way to Jerusalem, surrounded by crowds and teaching urgent things, and the disciples may have thought children an interruption. Some months earlier, in Capernaum, He had set a child in their midst as an example (Mark 9:36–37).

witnesses.matthew: Notes that the people asked Jesus to lay His hands on the children and pray, and that He did so before moving on. Matthew has already recorded Jesus’ call to become as little children (18:3), so here he lets the action speak.
witnesses.mark: Gives the strongest feeling and the warmest gesture: Jesus was “greatly displeased,” and He “took them up in His arms.” Mark pictured the same embrace when Jesus set a child among the Twelve (9:36).
witnesses.luke: Says they brought “infants” and sets the scene right after the Pharisee and the tax collector: the humble man and the babies in arms show that the kingdom is received, not earned. Here Luke rejoins Matthew and Mark after the long journey section found only in his Gospel (9:51–18:14).

seeing.reveals: Jesus makes room for those with no claim on His time. He is indignant when His own followers block the way, and He takes the smallest into His arms.
seeing.living: The kingdom is received the way a child receives a gift, with open hands and nothing to bargain with. Receive it that way yourself, and never stand between Jesus and those others think too small to matter.
seeing.ponder: Have you thought you must become something before you can come to Jesus? What would it mean to be carried to Him just as you are?

preaching.big_idea: Jesus welcomes the little ones, and only those who receive like them enter His kingdom.
outline: Disciples who got in the way (13)
preaching.watch_for: In all three Gospels the next scene is a man asking what he must do to inherit eternal life. The children did nothing and received the kingdom; the man who had kept the commandments went away sorrowful.
